item.title: Partially Decentralized Multi-Agent Q-Learning via Digital Cousins for Wireless Networks
item.description: arXiv:2503.05970v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Q-learning is a widely used reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm for optimizing wireless networks, but faces challenges with large state-spaces. Recently proposed multi-environment mixed Q-learning (MEMQ) algorithm addresses these challenges by employing multiple Q-learning algorithms across multiple synthetically generated, distinct but structurally related environments, so-called digital cousins. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-agent MEMQ (M-MEMQ) for cooperative decentralized wireless networks with multiple networked transmitters (TXs) and base stations (BSs). TXs do not have access to global information (joint state and actions). The new concept of coordinated and uncoordinated states is introduced. In uncoordinated states, TXs act independently to minimize their individual costs and update local Q-functions. In coordinated states, TXs use a Bayesian approach to estimate the joint state and update the joint Q-functions. The cost of information-sharing scales linearly with the number of TXs and is independent of the joint state-action space size. Several theoretical guarantees, including deterministic and probabilistic convergence, bounds on estimation error variance, and the probability of misdetecting the joint states, are given. Numerical simulations show that M-MEMQ outperforms several decentralized and centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) multi-agent RL algorithms by achieving 60% lower average policy error (APE), 40% faster convergence, 45% reduced runtime complexity, and 40% less sample complexity. Furthermore, M-MEMQ achieves comparable APE with significantly lower complexity than centralized methods. Simulations validate the theoretical analyses.
item.dc:creator: Talha Bozkus, Urbashi Mitra

item.title: Mechanistic Interpretability with Sparse Autoencoder Neural Operators
item.description: arXiv:2509.03738v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce sparse autoencoder neural operators (SAE-NOs), a new class of sparse autoencoders that operate in function spaces rather than fixed-dimensional Euclidean representations. We formalize the functional representation hypothesis, where data are explained through sparse compositions of structured functions. Unlike standard SAEs that represent concepts with scalar activations, SAE-NOs parameterize concepts as functions, enabling representations that capture not only a concept's presence, but also how and where it is expressed across the input domain. We achieve this through joint sparsity: concept sparsity selects active concepts, while domain sparsity governs where they are expressed. We instantiate this framework using Fourier neural operators (SAE-FNOs), parameterizing concepts as integral operators in the Fourier domain. This functional and spectral parameterization is particularly advantageous when data exhibit spatial structure across scales or when concepts are frequency-structured. We characterize SAE-FNO on vision data and demonstrate that it learns localized patterns, uses concepts more efficiently, and exhibits stable concept characteristics across sparsity levels. We further show that SAE-FNO adapts to changes in domain size and generalizes across discretizations, operating at resolutions beyond those seen during training, where standard SAEs fail. We also introduce lifting into SAEs and show theoretically and empirically that it acts as a preconditioner that accelerates optimization. Overall, our results show that moving from vector-valued to functional parameterizations, with concept and domain sparsity, extends SAEs from representing concept presence to modeling structured concept expression, highlighting the importance of parameterization.
item.dc:creator: Bahareh Tolooshams, Ailsa Shen, Anima Anandkumar

item.title: RJD-BASE: Multi-Modal Spectral Clustering via Randomized Joint Diagonalization
item.description: arXiv:2509.11981v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We revisit the problem of spectral clustering in multimodal settings, where each data modality is encoded as a graph Laplacian. While classical approaches--including joint diagonalization, spectral co-regularization, and multiview clustering--attempt to align embeddings across modalities, they often rely on costly iterative refinement and may fail to directly target the spectral subspace relevant for clustering. In this work, we introduce two key innovations. First, we bring the power of randomization to this setting by sampling random convex combinations of Laplacians as a simple and scalable alternative to explicit eigenspace alignment. Second, we propose a principled selection rule based on Bottom-$k$ Aggregated Spectral Energy (BASE)--a $k$-dimensional extension of the directional smoothness objective from recent minimax formulations--which we uniquely apply as a selection mechanism rather than an optimization target. The result is Randomized Joint Diagonalization with BASE Selection (RJD-BASE), a method that is easily implementable, computationally efficient, aligned with the clustering objective, and grounded in decades of progress in standard eigensolvers. Through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, we show that RJD-BASE reliably selects high-quality embeddings, outperforming classical multimodal clustering methods at low computational cost.
item.dc:creator: Haoze He, Artemis Pados, Daniel Kressner

item.title: Neural Signals Generate Clinical Notes in the Wild
item.description: arXiv:2601.22197v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generating clinical reports that summarize abnormal patterns, diagnostic findings, and clinical interpretations from long-term EEG recordings remains labor-intensive. We present CELM, the first clinical EEG-to-Language foundation model capable of summarizing long-duration, variable-length EEG recordings and performing end-to-end clinical report generation at multiple scales. CELM integrates pretrained EEG foundation models with language models to enable scalable multimodal learning. We curate a large-scale clinical EEG dataset containing 9,922 reports paired with approximately 11,000 hours of EEG recordings from 9,048 patients to train CELM, and release the benchmark pipeline, with automated report-structuring, to facilitate future research. Experimental results show that CELM consistently outperforms existing methods across all evaluation settings. Importantly, we further conduct human evaluation with clinical experts, demonstrating that CELM generates reports that are more clinically coherent, diagnostically reliable, and better aligned with expert interpretation. We release our model code and benchmark construction pipeline at https://github.com/Jathurshan0330/CELM.
item.dc:creator: Jathurshan Pradeepkumar, Zheng Chen, Jimeng Sun

item.title: CL-SEC: Cross-Layer Semantic Error Correction Empowered by Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2603.26125v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Achieving reliable communication has long been a fundamental challenge in networked systems. Semantic Error Correction (SEC) leverages the semantic understanding capabilities of language models (LMs) to perform application-layer error correction, complementing conventional channel decoding. While promising, existing SEC approaches rely solely on context captured by LMs at the application layer, ignoring the rich information available at the physical layer. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Cross-Layer SEC (CL-SEC), an LM-empowered error correction framework that integrates cross-layer information from both the physical and application layers to jointly correct corrupted words in text communication. Using a Bayesian combination in product form tailored to this framework, CL-SEC achieves significantly improved performance over methods that process information in isolated layers. CL-SEC shows substantial gains across multiple error-correction metrics, including bit-error rate, word-error rate, and semantic fidelity scores. Importantly, unlike most semantic communication systems that focus solely on recovering the semantic meaning of transmitted messages, CL-SEC aims to reconstruct the original transmitted message verbatim, leveraging the semantic understanding capabilities of LMs for precise reconstruction.
item.dc:creator: Yirun Wang, Yuyang Du, Soung Chang Liew, Yuchen Pan, Feifan Zhang, Lihao Zhang

item.title: 3D Point Splatting for mmWave Radar Novel View Synthesis
item.description: arXiv:2609.11894v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Solving novel view synthesis (NVS) for millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar requires a renderer that is physically faithful, complex-valued, and multi-viewpoint-tractable. No prior method achieves these three properties simultaneously. Differentiable Monte Carlo (MC) ray tracers implement the radar forward model directly with explicit material modeling and complex outputs, but a joint fit across views takes over an hour per scene. Optical-NVS ports of NeRF, hash grids, and 3D Gaussians train fast but discard phase and replace explicit material modeling with opaque learned features, restricting them to power-only range-azimuth (RA) magnitudes. We propose 3D Point Splatting (3DPS), the first differentiable point splatting renderer for radar, derived directly from the standard solid-angle form of the radar equation. Each oriented 3D point carries a material model built on ITU-R P.2040 permittivity and slab reflection, evaluated in closed form, with the resulting complex phasor splatted into range bins through a precomputed point spread function (PSF). The complex-valued output makes the renderer product-agnostic. The same optimized scene yields analog-to-digital converter (ADC), complex range profile (CRP), and RA outputs through standard fast Fourier transform (FFT) pipelines without retraining for each format. On six outdoor ColoRadar scenes, 3DPS reaches 0.587 mean Pearson correlation on held-out RA images. This is between 1.7x and 5.2x the three optical-NVS baselines (RadarSplat, Radar Fields, DART) and 1.3x the mmIR ray tracer at 1/25 of its wall-clock time. Training takes approximately 3 minutes per scene on a single RTX 4090. Project page: https://3d-point-splatting.github.io/
item.dc:creator: Adnan Armouti, Yixuan Gao, Rajalakshmi Nandakumar

item.title: From Winding-Fault Geometry to Reliability: Estimation and Prognosis of Stator Inter-Turn Faults
item.description: arXiv:2609.13448v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper develops an integrated framework for estimation, prognosis, and reliability assessment of stator inter-turn faults in induction motors. The fault is characterized by its severity, defined as the fraction of short-circuited turns, and its spatial orientation. A geometric fault model shows that the resulting output signature is affine in the fault severity and exhibits a fundamental spatial periodicity. Exploiting this structure, an augmented-state particle filter jointly estimates the nonlinear electromechanical state and the unknown fault severity while quantifying posterior uncertainty. The estimated degradation is then propagated using four prognostic models: linear trend, Holt exponential smoothing, Bayesian degradation, and particle-based forecasting. Their predictions are connected to threshold-crossing remaining useful life (RUL), first-passage reliability, degradation-dependent hazard reliability, and a Weibull lifetime benchmark, thereby providing both deterministic and probabilistic health assessments. Numerical results demonstrate accurate online fault estimation and output reconstruction, characterize the effects of degradation pattern and prediction horizon on prognosis, and show consistent reliability and threshold-crossing predictions. Moreover, estimation accuracy remains comparable across the distinct fault orientations induced by the spatial periodicity. The resulting framework provides a unified connection from physics-based inter-turn fault modeling to online diagnosis, degradation prognosis, and reliability assessment.
item.dc:creator: Bambang L. Widjiantoro, Syahrul Munir, Katherin Indriawati, Moh Kamalul Wafi

item.title: LWM-TF: A Wireless Foundation Model on 5G NR Time-Frequency Resource Grids
item.description: arXiv:2610.21013v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Received OFDM grids preserve both pilot and payload observations, yet wireless foundation models are rarely pre-trained on them. We introduce LWM-TF, a 9.58M-parameter factorized masked autoencoder pre-trained on complex 5G NR uplink grids taken after the FFT and before channel estimation. Each block attends first across OFDM symbols and then across resource blocks and receive antennas, and the mask follows the same two axes. Because the payload phase is unpredictable, the model reconstructs the normalized log-power of each masked token and predicts its scale separately; ablations show that the two terms are complementary and that this target outperforms complex-signal reconstruction. The encoder is pre-trained on 850,496 physical uplink shared channel (PUSCH) slots from a 10^6-slot dataset simulated with the NR transmit chain under various channel conditions. With the encoder frozen, linear probes classify modulation, predict CRC success, and detect UE mobility. On a separately generated test set, 16 labeled slots per class give 0.85 modulation accuracy, 0.82 CRC area under the ROC curve (AUROC), and 0.73 mobility AUROC, ahead of a supervised CNN on every paired draw. With 10,000 labels the probes reach 0.94, 0.96, and 0.92, well above engineered receiver statistics, and detect mobility where the CNN stays at chance. Without any impairment labels, distances in the frozen feature space flag unseen waveform impairments with 0.78 macro AUROC, against 0.68 for receiver statistics. A single pre-trained encoder thus provides receiver features that transfer across tasks, most strongly when labels are scarce.
item.dc:creator: Namhyun Kim, Sadjad Alikhani, Ahmed Alkhateeb

item.title: FastSAR: Open-Source SAR Image Formation on CPUs, GPUs, and TPUs, and a Matched Comparison of Algorithms, Precisions, and Processors
item.description: arXiv:2610.33932v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The number of spaceborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) collectors is growing exponentially, each returning raw collections that must be formed into images. Exact backprojection needs 1.6 trillion interpolated reads and 90 trillion floating-point operations for a 108-megapixel Umbra image. How long it takes to form an image, and at what price, depends on the algorithm, the arithmetic, and the hardware. Open-source implementations have never been compared on matched hardware against a common reference, and none run on Google tensor processing units (TPUs). This paper presents FastSAR, an open-source SAR image formation library for central processing units (CPUs), NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs), and TPUs. With it, we compare three SAR image formation algorithms, four floating-point formats, and six cloud devices in every supported combination, with cost per image at on-demand cloud prices as the fair common measure. FastSAR is 1.06 to 22,000 times faster than the tested open-source implementations at equal or better accuracy, and the full suite of hardware, algorithm, and floating-point combinations lets a user choose the Pareto-optimal configuration for their balance of accuracy, speed, and cost. The L4 GPU forms images the cheapest overall. Larger GPUs are faster but cost more per image because their price rises faster than their speed. The TPUs come close to the GPUs in cost, but only for the factorized algorithm, and the CPU is far less efficient in both speed and cost. Lower precision formats buy less of a speedup than expected, and each step down in precision costs accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Paul Singerman, Tom Braun

item.title: Non-intrusive appliance state detection in unseen homes using classical machine learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.00920v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) infers, from the aggregate signal of a single smart meter, when each appliance in a home is ON or OFF, offering significant potential to enhance energy efficiency. Classical machine-learning detectors report F1 scores (the harmonic mean of precision and recall) from 0.53 to 0.98, but the causes of this spread are unseparated, so it is unclear which design choices matter. Real-world deployments, however, require detectors that work in houses never seen during training, whereas most studies test on houses used for training. To address this challenge, we propose a factorial analysis of variance design that separates the effects of classifier, feature set and class-imbalance strategy across five appliances (270 configurations), and a leave-house-out protocol with house-grouped model selection. Unlike studies that vary one factor at a time or pool houses, the approach attributes performance to each factor and measures it on unseen homes. Extensive experiments on REFIT, a public dataset of 20 UK households, show that the appliance explains 38 percent of F1 variance, the feature set 13 percent, the classifier 8 percent and the imbalance strategy 2 percent. Pooled testing overstates support-weighted F1 (0.548 versus 0.447 in unseen houses), class weighting gains grow from 32 percent to 69 percent, and feature engineering gives the same 52 percent gain in both protocols. House-grouped selection raises F1 for three of five appliances, by up to 0.110, and a convolutional neural network scores 0.450 (0.496 calibrated) against 0.447 for classical models. The findings guide appliance-level monitoring in smart-metering and energy-management systems.

item.title: Flexible Piezoelectric Tactile Sensing System for Intelligent Object Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2611.07779v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tactile sensing provides information about object properties that can improve robotic grasping and manipulation. However, accurate object recognition during the early stages of grasping remains challenging, particularly under strict real-time constraints. This study presents a flexible, distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing system for early-stage object recognition. The system was experimentally evaluated using six everyday objects and three recognition approaches: feature-based classification using support vector machines (SVMs), raw-signal classification using 1D convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) and convolutional recurrent neural networks (C-RNNs), and spatiotemporal heatmap classification using a 2D-CNN. The effects of sensor count and temporal window size on recognition accuracy and real-time feasibility were systematically investigated. Increasing the number of sensing elements improved recognition performance across all approaches. The best-performing method, based on spatiotemporal heatmaps and a 2D-CNN, achieved F1-scores of 0.9796, 0.9846, and 0.9903 using 16, 24, and 32 sensors, respectively. The optimal configuration, comprising 32 sensors and a 100-ms temporal window (50 samples), was deployed on an embedded edge platform, achieving an end-to-end recognition latency of approximately 101 ms from contact onset and an energy consumption of 63.8 microjoules per inference. These results demonstrate the potential of distributed piezoelectric tactile sensing for accurate, energy-efficient, and real-time object recognition during robotic grasping.
